A single-atom alloy is a dilute alloy in which individual atoms of a reactive metal are dispersed in the surface of a more inert host metal, so that every minority atom is surrounded only by host atoms. Such isolated sites can carry out a step the host cannot (for example, dissociating a molecule), while the host determines what happens to the products. They are a limiting case of [bimetallic surfaces](/papers/topics/bimetallic-surfaces/), where ensemble effects are pushed to the single-atom limit.

## Isolated Pd atoms in Cu(111) and Au(111) (2009)

Tierney, Baber, Kitchin and Sykes made isolated Pd atoms in Cu(111) and Au(111) by depositing 0.01 monolayer of Pd, and imaged them with low-temperature STM; DFT showed that Pd alloys exothermically into both hosts and prefers to be surrounded by host atoms at low Pd fraction. The same Pd loading dissociated H2 on Cu but not on Au. DFT traced the difference to the host: H bound next to Pd is stable on Cu sites but not on Au sites, and the calculated H2 dissociation barrier over a Pd atom in Cu(111) was only about 0.02 eV, versus about 0.5 eV on Cu(111). They concluded that the host metal affects reactivity in a way that goes beyond dilution, electronic or geometric effects, and proposed computational surveys of host and dopant combinations to design such bifunctional catalysts ([Tierney et al. 2009](/papers/tierney2009/)). Summary: [tierney2009](/papers/tierney2009/). See also [Hydrogen spillover](/papers/topics/hydrogen-spillover/).
